content: Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC) is a severe complication in children with Hirschsprung's disease (HD), characterized by intestinal inflammation. Patients with HAEC often experience symptoms such as diarrhea, explosive stools, and abdominal distension. Probiotics, which are live microorganisms known to promote gut health, have been proposed as a potential intervention to optimize gastrointestinal function and improve gut flora. However, the effectiveness and safety of probiotics in preventing HAEC remain uncertain. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of probiotic supplementation, either alone or in combination with pharmacological treatments, on the prevention of HAEC. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, and others, up to February 27, 2022. Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles and reviews were examined to identify any additional trials. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing probiotics with placebo or other non-probiotic interventions for HAEC prevention were included. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the risk of bias in the included studies, resolving disagreements through discussion with a third reviewer. The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach, and odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for dichotomous outcomes. The analysis included two RCTs with a total of 122 participants. The overall risk of bias in these studies was judged to be high due to issues such as inadequate random sequence generation, allocation concealment, and lack of blinding. Additionally, the small sample size further reduced the reliability of the findings. The evidence regarding the effect of probiotics on the occurrence of HAEC was highly uncertain (OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.10 to 3.43; I² = 74%; 2 studies, 120 participants; very low-certainty evidence). One study did not report on serious adverse events, while the other study found no serious adverse events related to probiotics. Probiotics appeared to have little to no effect on the severity of HAEC at Grade I (OR 0.66, 95% CI 0.14 to 3.16; I² = 25%; 2 studies, 120 participants; low-certainty evidence). The evidence for the effect of probiotics on the severity of HAEC at Grade II was very uncertain (OR 1.14, 95% CI 0.01 to 136.58; I² = 86%; 2 studies, 120 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, probiotics seemed to have little to no effect on the severity of HAEC at Grade III (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.05 to 3.45; I² = 0%; 2 studies, 120 participants; low-certainty evidence). No overall mortality or withdrawals due to adverse events were reported in the included studies. Probiotics also appeared to have little to no effect on the recurrence of HAEC episodes compared to placebo (OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.24 to 3.00; 1 study, 60 participants; low-certainty evidence). In conclusion, the current evidence is insufficient to determine the efficacy or safety of probiotics for the prevention of Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis when compared to placebo. The low to very low certainty of the available evidence highlights the need for further well-designed and adequately powered randomized controlled trials to establish the true effectiveness of probiotics in this context.
